So, moving on:

I think you might be slightly misinformed about some of the aspects of bipolar disorder. First off, Bipolar disorder often doesn't present itself until the mid teenage years. Most people are diagnosed in their early 20s, but medical science is getting better at identifying it, and more importantly distinguishing it from things like ADHD, depression, and normal adolescent mood changes. People with mood and personality disorders of all kinds lead very successful lives, even people who are not treated. Regardless, ignoring the co-morbid disorders, bipolar disorder is not immediately endangering a child's life. Further someone who has a bipolar diagnosis who then has children will know to be cautious about it, and to look for the signs, and to seek treatment - just as they would with anything else that can happen to a child.

Another thing to consider is that there is a huge portion of people that develop bipolar disorder due to environmental factors, particularly childhood abuse and neglect. Even if no one diagnosed with bipolar disorder had children it would still persist in the population. Of course, it's a fallacy to suggest that it isn't immoral just because it will still happen.

What it comes down to, though, is whether or not an individual can be a successful parent despite bipolar disorder. I think that anybody who has children when they are not in a position to properly care for it is, on some level, being negligent. Knowing you will not be able to get help for your child should they develop bipolar disorder is no different than knowing you won't have the money to support your child. It's not child abuse, though. That requires actual present action. "Having a child" is not abuse; failing to care for them is. It's tempting to think that by accepting the 40% or so risk of your child developing bipolar is abuse, but there are millions of things that you can pass on. You are not giving your child bipolar disorder just because you are their parent any more than you are giving them diabetes, cancer, or hypertension when you are aware that it runs in your family.

It's fine if you think that having children when you know they are at risk for anything is immoral, but you can't single out bipolar disorder or even genetic things. My personal opinion is that it is not immoral unless there is severe impairment to the quality of life of the child; i.e., diseases that there are no treatments for and also that have a high risk of being passed down genetically.

Exactly. If it were capable of the amazing things that it's proponents have claimed, then we would already have amazing products from it. The fact that we don't do much with it suggests it really has few advantageous uses over other materials.

I've written about this material for many years. It was invented--or rather 'discovered'--in France in the 80s where it is known as Isochanvre and is in routine use there, as a by-product of the large industrial hemp industry there. It was originally reverse-engineered from Roman era concrete used in ancient bridges. It is in the class of geopolymers--cement and ceramic alternatives based on a silicon chemistry so-called because they form molecular chains similar to organic polymers. Hemp herd/chard is rich in silicon and in commercial production this is enhanced through a chemical siliconization process. It's not a wonder material, but it has many interesting properties that suit its use in green architecture. It's very resilient and can be tailored for a range of hardness from something like ceramic to something like linoleum. In lower density, which longer fiber lengths, it offers an insulation value akin to straw bale while being far stronger and immune to mold and animal infiltration. It can be used in formwork, made into blocks, used as a fill material in fachwerk or Japanese style earth/clay walls, or employed as a more resilient alternative rendering to plaster or adobe.

Even though it is in common use across Europe and is usually derived from industrial hemp that can't be smoked, it's use has been limited to ocassional experiments using imported material by the federal government suppression of all hemp use in the US. As long as it's limited to imported material, it can't really get a foothold in use here because it can't compete in cost. Farmers and, of course, hemp advocates have been fighting for decades to get it more widely known and used here. Now that pot growing is an emergent commercial industry in some states, it's going to start producing this large volume of herd by-product that people are going to want to make into other things. So we may see more use of this in the near future. If you can ship and sell hemp clothing around the country, it's hard to see how they could stop people from selling pre-made hempcrete mixes and blocks.
